blocks.nav: Who found the bust, and where exactly?
blocks.h: Who found the bust, and where exactly?
paras: The German Oriental Society's dig at Amarna, led by Ludwig Borchardt and paid for by the Berlin merchant James Simon, found it in house P 47.2, in a narrow room of 2 by 5.5 metres where a sculptor kept his models. Borchardt's

tells how. Called to the house soon after the midday break on 6 December 1912, he let his first foreman, Mohammed Ahmed es-Senussi, dig there alone while he directed him from close by. About knee-high in the rubble a painted neck came to light. "Lebensgroße bunte Büste der Königin", life-size painted bust of the queen, was called out and written down, and the work went on by hand. The bust was almost whole: the ears were chipped, and the left eye had no inlay. After midnight Borchardt wrote in his diary: "Beschreiben nützt nichts, ansehen", describing is no use, look.
An inscribed piece of ivory from a pit in the courtyard names the sculptor Thutmose, so the house is taken to be his workshop. Borchardt called that very likely, though not proven.
, on the east bank of the Nile about 270 kilometres south of Cairo as the crow flies, was the city King Akhenaten built in the 14th century BC, and
was his chief wife.

blocks.nav: Why is the division of 1913 disputed?
blocks.h: Why is the division of 1913 disputed?
paras: Because the two sides tell it differently: the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, which runs the Berlin museums, says the division was open and correct, while Egyptian archaeologists such as Zahi Hawass and Monica Hanna say the bust's worth was hidden from Egypt's side.

Under the rules of the time, a dig's finds were split between Egypt and the excavators. Borchardt made up the two halves, and Gustave Lefebvre, sent by Egypt's Antiquities Service, chose one on 20 January 1913. The half with a painted house altar showing the royal family went to Cairo, the half with the bust to James Simon, who gave it to the Berlin museums in 1920. Why Lefebvre chose as he did is not known, the
notes.

paras: In the Neues Museum on Berlin's Museum Island, the only object in the north dome room,
. In 2016 photographs were not allowed in that room, to protect the bust from light, and a copy that blind visitors may touch stood opposite it.

Simon first kept it in his villa. It was first shown in the Neues Museum on 1 April 1924. In the Second World War it was moved for safety, in the end to a salt mine at Merkers in Thuringia, where US troops found it in 1945. It came back to West Berlin in 1956 and has stood in the Neues Museum again since the building reopened in October 2009, the
records.
From the excavator's own report, from the papers of the division, and from what each side has said, with its date.

Borchardt's report of 1923 tells the find in his own words, drawing on his diary, with plans of the house and the room and the measured spot where the bust lay. It also prints Friedrich Rathgen's tests of the paints. The papers of the find and the division are held in Berlin, and Friederike Seyfried published a detailed record of them in 2010,
What stays open is what Egypt's inspector knew when he chose, why he chose as he did, and whether the left eye ever had an inlay.

paras: In a sculptor's house, in the room where he kept his models.

The left eye had no inlay when the bust was found, and none turned up in the sifted rubble. Borchardt was sure it never had one: the socket shows no trace of glue and was never hollowed out for an inlay. Some scholars think it was lost or destroyed, and other portraits of her show both eyes.
Its core is limestone, with painted layers of plaster on top, and the scan of 2006 found a carved face beneath them.
Tests of its paints and CT scans match ancient work. In 2009 both Berlin's Egyptian Museum and Zahi Hawass rejected the claim.
